_comment: The guided tour (tour.js in the app, tour.html as slides and PDF). One file drives all three, so the words are written once. In the app the tour is a walk through the site: each view a step opens is a stop, where a card names the step, gives its headline and says what to try (hint). A headline is one figure (value, label) or a comparison (figures, each with its label), and may lead with a claim it supports and say what was measured (measure); a step that opens no view is one card on its own. Numbers are never typed here: a {placeholder} is filled at runtime from data/boundary_evidence.json and the published journey-times index (tourFigureValues in tour.js), so a weekly rebuild cannot leave the tour quoting stale figures. Every money or planning claim names its source and the date it was checked. preview_only keeps the tour behind ?preview=1 until its copy is approved. Titles, leads and the opening were chosen by the maintainer on 20 October 2026; the points under each step were picked by the maintainer in the 'Tour copy review' doc on 20 October 2026.

opening.headline: Passengers deserve one network. This one is built from open data.
opening.lead: On this coast, four bus companies run four apps and their own day tickets, and two councils plan up to a line through Portslade. This proof of concept joins it all up from the government's open bus data, and measures how the buses really run.

steps.title: What passengers face today
steps.lead: Four operators each run their own apps and tickets. With a council boundary through the community, services in the west are weaker on every measure.

headline.claim: The council border between West Sussex and Brighton & Hove has a measurable impact on passenger services west of the line.
headline.measure: Average weekday buses per stop, over every stop within 4 km of the line along the coast. The west gets {band_share}% of the east's service.

figures.label: West of the line, in West Sussex
East of the line, in Brighton & Hove

points: Weekday departures per stop: {band_west_dps} west of the line against {band_east_dps} east, in a band 4 km either side ({band_share}%).
Routes on a weekday: {routes_west_weekday} against {routes_east_weekday}. On Saturday {routes_west_sat} against {routes_east_sat}; on Sunday {routes_west_sun} against {routes_east_sun}.
Departures after 11pm on a weekday: {late_west} west of the line against {late_east} east.
Lancing and South Portslade, about five miles apart on the same coast road: {lancing_dps} against {sportslade_dps} weekday departures per stop.
Joint working pays: up to 43% more passengers on the two routes the councils improved together. The coast west of Portslade wasn't one of them.

steps.title: The network as people use it
steps.lead: Each operator's buses on one map and one departure board. Every operator's ticket zones in one place, and a cross-operator journey checker.

Every operator's day-ticket zones on one map, and a checker that finds the cheapest ticket that covers a whole journey, across companies.
Door-to-door planning across operators, still experimental.

steps.title: What the buses actually did
steps.lead: The same open feed, kept: real journey times, where buses lose time, and how reliable each route is, published for anyone to check.

headline.label: of the live feed kept and matched to the timetable

points: Each minute the live feed is saved, and each bus is matched to the timetabled journey it is running.
Journey times between any two stops, by day and time of day, with the slow end shown as well as the usual.
A delay map of where buses lose time against the timetable; a stretch is only coloured once it has enough journeys behind it.
Gaps in the record are listed, not hidden: {recorded_gaps}.

try.label: Worthing to Portslade, measured
try.hint: Each dot is one bus we timed from Worthing to Portslade, across the council line. The solid line is the usual time and the dashed line the timetable. Change the day or the time of day to compare.

try.label: Where buses lose time
try.hint: Each stretch is coloured by the time buses lose there. Tap one for its figures.

steps.title: Beyond the baseline
steps.lead: ABOD, the Department's free analytics service, is for officers with an invitation. This is for everyone: the same kind of evidence, plus passenger tools, under an open licence.

headline.label: of tracked journeys named by the operator's own feed

badge.label: From ABOD's published code and documents

points: Anyone can open it: no login, no invitation. Councillors, passengers and journalists see the same figures.
It joins the evidence to the passenger side: live times for every operator, every operator's ticket zones, and the cheapest ticket across them.

ABOD matches a bus to its journey by the operator's journey reference and skips it when that does not match the timetable. This site tries three ways, reads the trip feed as well as the location feed, and names {identified_share}% of tracked journeys by the operator's own feed.
ABOD's code can be read on GitHub, but its licence lets only KPMG firms reuse it. This site's code is MIT-licensed: anyone may copy it.

steps.title: Public money, public return
steps.lead: The data is free from the Bus Open Data Service; everything else costs under £20 a year. Open-source software at its finest: any developer can spin up the most powerful bus information resource in their area.

headline.label: a year to run: the data is free, and so is the hosting

points: Every figure on this site is built on that data, on free hosting, for under £20 a year: the cost of the web address.

sources.label: PublicTechnology: DfT to spend £37m on real-time bus data service (4 September 2023)
ITS UK: Department for Transport chooses Kainos to run the Bus Open Data Service (17 November 2025)

steps.title: How far to trust it
steps.lead: Every figure says what it was divided by, how it was made, and what would make it wrong.

headline.claim: The live times on this site are closer to when the bus really leaves than the timetable is.
headline.measure: How often each was within the accuracy window the Real Time Information Group (RTIG) recommends, replayed over 28 recorded days (25 September to 24 October).

points: As the board actually showed them, minute by minute, 79% of live times were within RTIG's window, and 86% of departures had a live time 15 minutes before they were due. We publish how often we are wrong, nightly, on the live data health page.
Good to about a minute, not a second; fewer than 10 journeys over 5 days shows "too few", never a number.
{identified_share}% of {identified_tracked} tracked journeys are matched to their journey by the operator's own feed.
We are timing buses by hand to check our stop times; the result will be published here.
A bus we did not see is "missing", never "cancelled": its tracker may simply have been off.

sources.label: Live-estimate accuracy: a replay of 20 recorded days (16 October 2026)

steps.title: What one coast shows
steps.lead: If one volunteer can do this for one coast, an authority or a partner can do it for a region. The template is coming; the code is already open.

headline.label: for anyone to use, distribute or edit

points: The data is national; only the questions are local.
Open by default: MIT-licensed code, CC BY words and data, and every day's evidence archived in public.
A template for other regions is on the way, and a company that wants to develop this further would have full support.

steps.title: Let's build it together
steps.lead: The code is open and the data is public. Operators: check our figures. Councils: plan the coast as one corridor. Technology firms and other regions: help turn this into a template.
